title: Cross-engine — same host, current-main MyVector
subtitle: MyVector (current main: PR #278 + #280) · vsql_vector · pgvector · MariaDB — fashion-mnist-784, all four on one A1 host, identical cores & cache-above-index
nav: ★ executive summary · cross-engine (A2) · MyVector by version · glove (cosine) · village
description: The fair, apples-to-apples cross-engine view, re-measured 2026-11-10 under controlled conditions: current-main MyVector (PR #278 vectorized kernels + keepPrunedConnections, and PR #280 which removed the ANN-rewrite overhead), vsql_vector (VillageSQL), pgvector (Postgres 17), MariaDB 12.3 — all four on the same A1 host, each pinned to the same 4 cores, each with its working set cached above the ~188 MB index, run one-at-a-time, on fashion-mnist-784-euclidean (60k × 784, L2) vs published ground truth. At matched recall@10 (the table below) MyVector now leads ~2–3×; see the caveats for why this reverses the earlier figures on this page.
caveats: This is a fresh controlled re-run (2026-11-10) that supersedes the earlier numbers on this page, which were wrong for two reasons: (1) they were measured on MyVector's pre-#280 build, and (2) the sweep ran while the A1 host was loaded, which throttled throughput unevenly. Re-measuring everything together — current main, all engines pinned to the same 4 cores, each cache-sized above the index, run sequentially — gives the honest picture. We also caught and fixed a fairness bug mid-run: pgvector's first pass used its default 128 MB shared_buffers, which thrashed the 188 MB index; with shared_buffers=2 GB it is ~50% faster (ef=50 552→810 QPS) and that corrected figure is what's shown.

The honest read (matched recall@10 — the table above): with #278 (recall-per-ef now on pgvector's curve) and #280 (ANN-rewrite overhead removed, a measured +48–80% at low ef), MyVector serves the most QPS at every matched-recall point — e.g. ~2695 vs pgvector 1343 / vsql 1176 at recall 0.975, and ~2143 vs MariaDB 965 / pgvector 810 at recall 0.998. The earlier version of this page showed MyVector trailing ~2× at low recall; that gap was the per-query rewrite overhead, which #280 has since largely removed. The remaining engine-side overhead (JSON_TABLE round-trip) is designed out in RFC-006.

Cache parity (essential for fairness): each engine's working set sits above the ~188 MB index — MyVector holds its HNSW graph in its own process memory; pgvector shared_buffers=2 GB; vsql InnoDB buffer pool 4 GB (its default pool thrashes to ~2 QPS otherwise); MariaDB InnoDB pool 2 GB + mhnsw_max_cache_size=1 GiB. All four pinned to cores 12–15 and run one-at-a-time so no engine contends with another.

Dataset / params: fashion-mnist-784-euclidean (ann-benchmarks, 60k×784, L2), HNSW M=16, ef_construction=200 (MyVector + pgvector + vsql; MariaDB MHNSW fixes ef_construction at 10 internally). Recall@10 vs published exact neighbors. Warm ef_search sweep (500 queries/point); headline cards = warm ef_search=200.

MariaDB builds its HNSW online during load (~209 s) and is the 2nd-fastest searcher here; in this run its ef=10 point is monotonic (1427 QPS > ef=20's 1233) so all points are kept (unlike earlier runs where its ef_search floor made the sub-floor point anomalous).
Index build: MyVector 68 s · pgvector 74 s · vsql 164 s · MariaDB 209 s — MyVector's build is the fastest of the four.

Honest limits: this is a same-host run on a shared A1 box (controlled via core-pinning + sequential runs + settle, but not a dedicated quiet machine), and each engine uses its own result-collection harness (all server-side timed — MyVector/MariaDB via SELECT NOW(6) brackets, pgvector/vsql via the client's timing). The method is disclosed so the numbers can be reproduced; treat a 2–3× as 'clearly ahead', not a precise ratio.
